{{Short description|Theorem in mathematics}}

In mathematics, the '''Weierstrass Nullstellensatz''' is a version of the [[intermediate value theorem]] over a [[real closed field]]. It says:<ref>R. G. Swan, Tarski's Principle and the Elimination of Quantifiers at [https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~swan/expo/index.html Richard G. Swan], Theorem 10.4.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Srivastava |first1=Shashi Mohan |title=A Course on Mathematical Logic |date=2013 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4614-5746-6 |language=en|contribution=Proposition 5.9.11}}</ref>
:Given a [[polynomial]] <math>f</math> in one variable with coefficients in a real closed field ''F'' and <math>a < b</math> in <math>F</math>, if <math>f(a) < 0 < f(b)</math>, then there exists a <math>c</math> in <math>F</math> such that <math>a < c < b</math> and <math>f(c) = 0</math>.

== Proof ==
Since ''F'' is real-closed, ''F''(''i'') is algebraically closed, hence ''f''(''x'') can be written as <math>u\prod_i(x-\alpha_i)</math>, where <math>u\in F</math> is the leading coefficient and <math>\alpha_j\in F(i)</math> are the roots of ''f''. Since each nonreal root <math>\alpha_j=a_j+ib_j</math> can be paired with its conjugate <math>\overline\alpha_j=a_j-ib_j</math> (which is also a root of ''f''), we see that ''f'' can be factored in ''F''[''x''] as a product of linear polynomials and polynomials of the form <math>(x-\alpha_j)(x-\overline\alpha_j)=(x-a_j)^2+b_j^2</math>, <math>b_j\ne0</math>.

If ''f'' changes sign between ''a'' and ''b'', one of these factors must change sign. But <math>(x-a_j)^2+b_j^2</math> is strictly positive for all ''x'' in any formally real field, hence one of the linear factors <math>x-\alpha_j</math>, <math>\alpha_j\in F</math>, must change sign between ''a'' and ''b''; i.e., the root <math>\alpha_j</math> of ''f'' satisfies <math>a<\alpha_j<b</math>.
